surveys.narrative: LAT ABUNDANCE WAS FAIR, WITH ALL FISH COLLECTED BETWEEN 17 AND 23 IN. NO FISH FROM ANY YEAR CLASS MORE RECENT THAN 1986 WERE COLLECTED, BUT THE SAMPLE SIZE WAS SMALL AND YEAR CLASSES COULD EASILY HAVE BEEN MISSED. LAT GROWTH WAS ABOUT AVERAGE FOR COOK COUNTY. WAE ABUNDANCE WAS LOW COMPARED TO PAST ASSESSMENTS. ONLY ONE FISH WAS COLLECTED; 25.9 IN AND AGE VI. BACK-CALCULATED LENGTHS FROM THIS SINGLE FISH APPEARED TO INDICATE BETTER THAN AVERAGE GROWTH. TLC ABUNDANCE APPEARED TO HAVE DECLINED SINCE 1980 AND 1976, WHEN CPUE'S WERE 7.5 AND 5.2 FISH/GILL NET, RESPECTIVELY. ALL TLC COLLECTED IN THIS ASSESSMENT WERE IN THE 7 IN RANGE.

Magnetic Lake has about average populations of Lake Trout, N Pike and Walleyes as compared to statewide catch medians. A good population of small Ciscoes was indicated. Only a few Perch and one Bass were taken, but these two species may not have been accurately sampled.

Magnetic Lake is a 446-acre lake located on the U.S-Canadian border in Cook County, Minnesota. Access to the lake is through a broad channel connected from Gunflint Lake and is a popular travel route for recreationalist entering the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness (BWCAW). Magnetic Lake has seen minimal sampling over the past 50 years; however, more routine habitat monitoring has found suitable conditions for coldwater species like lake trout. Currently, Magnetic Lake is managed for lake trout and walleye with a goal for lake trout to maintain a minimum gill net catch of 1.0 fish/net. In 2025, a standard survey was conducted on Magnetic Lake using gillnets to monitor the current fish community.

Lake trout catch rates in gillnets were 0.6 fish/net and similar to previous surveys; however, slightly below the management goal. Low catch rates are not uncommon for summer lake trout surveys, especially in lakes with suspended coldwater forage like cisco. Lake trout lengths ranged from 12.2 to 22.2 inches and exhibited slow growth. Anglers may have a difficult time catching lake trout since they are low in abundance within Magnetic Lake.

Walleye catch rates in 2025 were 1.2 fish/net and had slightly increased from the previous survey from 1991 (0.2 fish/net). Six walleye were captured and ranged from 10.8 to 22.0 inches and represented three different age classes. Walleye growth was relatively fast likely due to cisco being present as a quality forage base. Anglers looking to target walleye should not expect to catch walleye easily, but rather, work a little harder to catch medium sized fish.

Other species encountered during the survey included a mix of cold and warm water fish species. Cisco catches were high at 7.2 fish/net and provide quality forage opportunities for lake trout and large walleye. Smallmouth bass, rock bass, white sucker, burbot, and yellow perch were also caught during the survey, but were present in low numbers.

Temperature and dissolved oxygen parameters were measured to monitor coldwater fish habitats during stressful summer periods. These results indicated there was approximately 43.0 feet of optimal habitat for lake trout (temperature < 8.8°C and dissolved oxygen > 3.0 ppm) in Magnetic Lake. This range of habitat was found at depths from 39.7 to 82.0 feet and further supports coldwater species like lake trout, burbot and cisco.

Minnesota Lakes within Cook County continue to be susceptible to aquatic invasive species introductions. Invasive species have the potential to significantly alter fish communities and overall lake health. Anglers should clean watercraft and fishing gear, drain all water, and dispose of unused bait in the trash to prevent accidental introductions.

Temperature and dissolved oxygen (DO) measurements were collected from the deepest basin in Magnetic Lake on August 13th, 2025, to evaluate the quantity and quality of cold, oxygenated water (i.e., oxythermal habitat) available to Lake Trout, the most sensitive coldwater species present in this lake (Cisco, also known as 'Tullibee', are also present). During the summer, Lake Trout require a layer of oxythermal habitat that contains water temperatures below 8.8 degrees C (47.8 degrees F) and dissolved oxygen concentrations above 3.0 mg/L. Based on the profile from the deepest basin (maximum sampled depth 80.4 feet), the water temperature decreased below 8.8 degrees C (47.8 degrees F) at 35.3 feet and the dissolved oxygen concentration stayed greater than 3.0 mg/L at 80.4 feet at the time of sampling. The thickness of this layer of water in the water column was 45.1 feet, indicating that oxythermal habitat was present for Lake Trout.

Further, the temperature at which dissolved oxygen decreased to 3.0 mg/L (i.e., TDO3, a single variable to characterize oxythermal habitat) was never reached because dissolved oxygen remained above 3.0 mg/L throughout the sampled depths. In this case, the minimum temperature, 5.9 degrees C (42.6 degrees F), was substituted as TDO3. TDO3 values cooler than 8.8 degrees C (47.8 degrees F) indicate that oxythermal conditions were suitable for Lake Trout at the time of the survey.

Data collected by the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources during the late summer period of maximum oxythermal stress (July 26th to Aug 24th) in 3 years, between 1976-2024, also indicate suitable oxythermal habitat in all years surveyed, with the least favorable conditions recorded in 2024 when the suitable oxythermal habitat layer was 38.8 feet thick. When inadequate oxythermal habitat is available, Lake Trout are squeezed into unfavorable, warmer water conditions and experience higher levels of stress.
